This allows the model to combine partial results correctly without ever storing the full quadratic score matrix in main memory.

Because the math remains consistent, the outputs match standard attention to floating-point tolerance—it’s an IO optimization, not an approximation trade-off.

scenario.notes: Relative position emerges from the rotation's inner product.

results.response:
Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) work by rotating query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their absolute position [Su et al., RoFormer (2021)]. When calculating attention scores, the product of the rotated query and key causes the absolute rotations to cancel out, leaving only the difference in position between the two tokens [Su et al., RoFormer (2021)].

This mechanism creates a relative encoding implemented through absolute rotations, meaning the model relies on the distance between tokens rather than fixed grid coordinates [Su et al., RoFormer (2021)]. Because the relative spacing remains consistent regardless of where tokens fall in the sequence, the model generalizes better to sequence lengths it hasn't seen during training [Su et al., RoFormer (2021)]. Unlike learned embeddings that might fail outside the training window, this geometric property holds for any offset.

A practical side effect is that you can pack several documents into one sequence without resetting position IDs, as the offsets cancel in the same way, so the model sees the same relative distances it would in an unpacked batch [Su et al., RoFormer (2021)].

Now that you see how the rotation cancels out, have you tried visualizing how the angle changes as the sequence length increases?
